Neonates of Cunningham's skink (Egernia cunninghami) emerge from their incubating eggs after a developmental period that depends strongly on thermal conditions. Eggs incubated at a mean temperature of 29.3202 °C [T = 29.3202 °C] produce hatchlings after 105 days [ab = 105 days], a duration that is broadly consistent with incubation times reported for other large-bodied Australian scincids under similar thermal regimes. Newborn individuals measure approximately 6.92 centimeters [Lb = approximately 6.92 centimeters] in snout-vent length and have a wet body mass averaging 7.73 grams [Wwb = 7.73 grams] immediately following emergence. This relatively modest size at birth is typical of the genus, reflecting a life-history strategy that prioritizes offspring number over individual neonatal mass. The hatchlings exhibit fully developed scales and locomotor capabilities, allowing them to begin foraging on small arthropods within days of eclosion. Field observations from the Weetangera region during the early 1990s provided the temperature data used to calibrate these incubation parameters.

As juvenile Cunningham's skinks grow, they undergo a prolonged period of somatic development before reaching reproductive maturity. The onset of gonadal activation, marking the transition to a reproductively viable adult, occurs at a snout-vent length of 19 centimeters [Lp = 19 centimeters], which represents the size at which individuals attain puberty. At this stage, the body mass of a typical individual reaches approximately 201.1 grams [Wwp = approximately 201.1 grams], reflecting the allometric scaling relationship between linear size and mass in this species. Continued growth beyond this point proceeds at a decelerating rate, with the ultimate snout-vent length of 24 centimeters [Li = 24 centimeters] representing the asymptotic maximum recorded in wild adult populations. This final size is attained only after several years, as growth rates slow considerably following sexual maturation.

The reproductive biology of Cunningham's skink is characterized by low annual fecundity relative to many other scincid lizards. Under average body temperature conditions of 22.09023 °C [T = 22.09023 °C], females achieve a maximum reproductive rate equivalent to 8 offspring per year [Ri = 8 offspring per year]. This modest output is partitioned across one, or occasionally two, litters per year, each consisting of between two and five live-born young. The extended gestation period and the production of fully formed neonates rather than eggs represent a substantial energetic investment per offspring, which is reflected in the relatively large size of the young at birth. Comparative data from sympatric congeners suggest that this low reproductive rate is offset by high offspring survival, likely facilitated by the complex social structure and communal denning behavior observed in this species.

Longevity records for Cunningham's skink indicate that this species is among the longest-lived of the Australian scincids. A well-documented individual observed by Harlow and cited in Stow (2004) was still reproductively active at 43 years [am = 43 years] of age, corresponding to a total documented lifespan of 15,695 days [am = 15,695 days] at a mean body temperature of 22.09023 °C [T = 22.09023 °C]. This exceptional longevity is accompanied by a slow life-history pace, with individuals requiring more than four years to reach first reproduction. Based on a detailed analysis of average body temperature data from the Barwicks field site, the age at first successful breeding event is estimated at approximately 1,612 days after hatching [tR = approximately 1,612 days after hatching], a figure derived from adding 1,507 days of post-hatching development to the 105-day incubation period at 29.3202 °C [T = 29.3202 °C]. This delayed maturation is consistent with the pattern of iteroparous, low-fecundity reproduction seen in many long-lived lizards.

The maximum adult body mass in Egernia cunninghami is tightly linked to skeletal size, with larger individuals attaining a wet weight of approximately 363.4 grams [Wwi = approximately 363.4 grams] at the asymptotic snout-vent length of 24 centimeters [Li = 24 centimeters]. Field data indicate that this mass varies substantially between seasons: males in the post-breeding period often carry increased fat reserves, while gravid females temporarily exceed this asymptotic mass during gestation before returning to baseline levels after parturition. The pronounced variation in body condition among adults of equivalent structural size reflects differences in social rank within the complex hierarchical groups that characterize this species' social system, with dominant individuals typically maintaining higher relative mass than subordinates.
